text: Forty-four minutes arguing that the industrial city is a mistake and the suburb is its correction. The City was made in 1939, when that proposition still carried the confidence of engineering rather than the sourness of hindsight: crowding, soot and poverty on one side of the ledger, and on the other a house with space around it and a family inside. Willard Van Dyke's documentary belongs to a practice that considered itself useful — images made to persuade planners and committees, not only audiences. The interest now lies in watching the assumptions get assembled in the open, in the order their makers found most convincing: air, children, traffic, and how far a man should have to travel to work. It is a pitch for a way of living, made before anyone had lived it long enough to complain.

Two men, one fence, and a flock of prize birds with an appetite for the seed bed next door. Pass the Gravy sets its feud in the narrowest available territory and then does something crueller than escalate it: the children of the two households announce an engagement, and the fathers are obliged to be civil. Leo McCarey builds the rest around a dinner table, the one piece of furniture that seats everybody facing everybody and lets nobody leave. What follows is a study in how a secret travels across a small group, one guest at a time. Max Davidson plays the host, saddled with running a reconciliation dinner as the news moves down the table. Twenty-three minutes, and most of the comedy is in what faces do while mouths are busy.

It was shot on colour stock, at sixteen frames a second, by the man who ran a camera shop in town. Almost nobody has seen it that way. Newsreels copied Barney Elliott's Kodachrome onto black-and-white 35mm and often ran it at the wrong speed, so the version lodged in public memory is greyer and faster than what he actually exposed. Elliott had been filming the bridge since it was under construction, which makes these eight minutes less an accident than the last instalment of a local project. What the reel holds is a roadway in motion and Leonard Coatsworth walking off it, having left his car where it stood. Engineering and physics classes still run the footage as a cautionary lesson; the Library of Congress put it in the National Film Registry in 1998. Two uses for the same eight minutes, neither one Elliott planned.

A country asks women into its shipyards and mines, and five years later asks them to leave. Connie Field's documentary takes both halves of that request seriously, which is rarer than it sounds: wartime work is easy to film as an emergency and harder to treat as a career people were building and expected to keep. Sixty-five minutes on factory floors, dockyards, pay, and the way a job alters what a woman thinks she is entitled to want next. The peacetime half is where it turns cold, since the institutions that ran the recruitment ran the reversal too. It was finished in 1980, near enough to the war that the women could still give their own account of it, and far enough that they had four decades to work out what the ending of it had cost.

One man plays every part, and the film lets him share the frame with himself. Sid Laverents is performer and filmmaker both: ten minutes of one-man-band music, cut fast and shot from several angles, so that the arrangement and the editing turn out to be the same job. Amateur is the technically accurate word for this and the misleading one. The labour of matching a body to itself take after take, keeping time with a version of yourself already on film, is not an excuse for the picture; it is its subject, and the reason the jokes land where they do. The Library of Congress added it to the National Film Registry for 2000, putting a one-man production on a list with pictures that needed a studio and a payroll. Multiplication is the joke and also the method.

The scene partner is a mannequin, and the actress is playing to it at full melodramatic pitch. I, an Actress runs nine minutes: a performer works through a scene at the top of her range while the director stays audible, close, and unable to keep out of it. George Kuchar made it in 1977, and the comedy lives in the distance between an emotional register borrowed from studio pictures and a set consisting of whatever happened to be in the room. It is filed as documentary, comedy and drama at once, and all three claims hold, which is a fair measure of how unstable the thing is. Rehearsal footage usually stays private for a reason. Here the camera keeps running while something real is pulled out of a person, and nine minutes turns out to be long enough for that to become the event.

Firdaus deals blackjack, and the film gives her shift the length it actually has. Nina Menkes sets two tired systems beside each other: the casino floor, lit around the clock and arranged so that nothing ever concludes, and the desert town outside it, an oasis going to seed, where a neighbour's violence carries through the wall. Her husband is missing. The film refuses the momentum a missing person usually supplies and declines to treat it as a puzzle; what accumulates instead is repetition, one correctly executed procedure after another, until the anger underneath becomes legible without being stated. Seventy-seven minutes, most of them spent watching a woman do a job properly. The pressure comes from how long the camera is prepared to wait.

A drunk with several names and a missionary with one share a small group of islands, and neither has anywhere else to be. Vessel of Wrath puts Ginger Ted and Miss Jones inside an arrangement neither chose: cholera breaks out, a hospital in an outlying part of the Alas Islands has to be staffed, and the two least compatible people available are the ones sent. The setting does the structural work — a place small enough that reputation is the only currency in circulation, and there is no other boat. The film is listed as comedy, drama and romance in that order, which is close to the order in which it uses them. Ninety-two minutes on the durability of disapproval, and on what becomes of a moral position when the work suddenly requires the man it was aimed at.

In 1959 a composer in Chicago finished a film announcing that jazz was over. Edward O. Bland's essay is polemic first and music film second: it argues about race and musical form in the same breath, treating the structure of a chorus as a claim about American life and the exhaustion of that structure as a forecast. The argument is spoken straight out, in the manner of a lecture that expects to be disagreed with. Around it sits the other reason to watch: the Arkestra working Chicago nightclubs in black and white, John Gilmore on tenor, and the only footage known to exist of Sun Ra from the years he spent in that city. Thirty-four minutes in which a prediction and the evidence against it are playing in the same room.

Muybridge photographed animals to learn how they moved, then turned the same apparatus on people. Thom Andersen's hour keeps four things in one line of thought — a life, a decade, an argument about what cinema is, and a slower question about what happens when a person is set against a blank background and asked to walk. The locomotion studies of the 1870s are the famous part, and they get their due as a forerunner of everything that followed. Andersen is more interested in the later work: grids of assorted people performing ordinary actions for a camera that had already decided how to sort them. Made in 1975, and the theory in it is not an overlay on the material. It is what the photographs were doing on their own.

A lecture on the reproductive habits of a small aquatic animal, delivered to a ladies' club by a man whose live specimens have not arrived. The Sex Life of the Polyp gives Dr. Benchley eleven minutes, a set of prepared pictures, and a subject complicated by the fact that polyps change sex from time to time — a detail he must get across to this particular audience without appearing to relish it. Almost nothing occurs on screen. The comedy is a matter of a voice under strain: the pause, the throat cleared, the extra clause bolted onto a sentence that should have ended two words ago. It is a talk given badly and built with precision, and the pleasure lies in watching authority come apart while the speaker keeps insisting on the scientific interest of his slides.

Thirteen shots, thirteen lakes, and in every frame the horizon runs straight through the middle. James Benning fixes the rule first and lets American weather supply the rest: since the composition never varies, everything that does — light, wind, chop, a boat, whatever crosses the water — arrives as event. Divide the runtime by the count and each lake gets roughly ten minutes, which removes any judgement about which of these places deserves more attention. What the film alters is the scale of what registers as something happening. Eight minutes into a fixed frame of water, a distant hull is a plot. The scheme is stubborn, and the stubbornness is what makes the looking possible; a viewer either gives in early or spends a hundred and thirty-five minutes resisting.

A train leaves the station, gathers speed, and the window it frames stops behaving like a window. Robert Breer opens Fuji with live footage — a bespectacled tourist, smiling, presumably Western — and then works the passing view down to its components: power lines, rails, the repeated pitch of rooflines, and at last the long oblique that is the mountain. Eight minutes of animation in which the drawn image keeps sliding back toward the photographic one, so that neither is ever a place to settle. No dialogue, no need for any. The pleasure comes from recognition arriving a beat late: a shape reads as geometry first and as a mountain second, and Breer keeps changing the order. Holding it together is the train, something moving past at a fixed rate, which is also a fair description of film through a projector.

Some of the children on screen are not performing; they were on shift when the camera arrived. The Cry of the Children builds a melodrama about child labour and then cuts in footage shot inside a working mill, so a story with a villain and a moral keeps being interrupted by fact. That mixture is what made it contentious in 1912, and it is still uncomfortable, though not in the way its makers intended: the documentary material shows up the thinness of the fiction, and the fiction is what got the documentary material into theatres. Twenty-nine minutes, and the most persuasive passages are the ones nobody staged — small bodies among large machines, carrying no rhetoric at all, doing the work the intertitles are straining to do.
